prompt:
A *group* $(G,*)$ is a set with an associative binary operation $*$ that has an identity element $e$ ($e*a=a*e=a$ for all $a$) and in which every $a$ has an inverse $a^{-1}$ ($a*a^{-1}=a^{-1}*a=e$). Powers are $a^n=a*\dots*a$ ($n$ factors), $a^0=e$, $a^{-n}=(a^{-1})^n$, so $a^{m+n}=a^m*a^n$ and $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$. $G$ is *finite* if it has finitely many elements; $|G|$ is its *order*. The *order* $\operatorname{ord}_G(g)$ of an element $g$ is the smallest positive integer $n$ with $g^n=e$. A subset $H\subseteq G$ is a *subgroup* if $a*b\in H$ and $a^{-1}\in H$ for all $a,b\in H$ (then $H$ is itself a group). For $g\in G$, $\langle g\rangle=\{e,g,g^2,\dots\}$.

Let $T=\{1,2,\dots,6\}$ be the group of nonzero residues modulo $7$ under multiplication mod $7$ (for example $2*3=6$ and $4*5=6$ since $20=2\cdot7+6$).

Find the inverses and the orders of $3$, $5$ and $6$ in $T$.

solutions.title: Compute
solutions.body: $3\cdot5=15\equiv1$, so $3^{-1}=5$ and $5^{-1}=3$; $6\cdot6=36\equiv1$, so $6^{-1}=6$. Powers of $3$ mod $7$: $3,2,6,4,5,1$, so $\operatorname{ord}(3)=6$. Powers of $5$: $5,4,6,2,3,1$, so $\operatorname{ord}(5)=6$. Powers of $6$: $6,1$, so $\operatorname{ord}(6)=2$.

answer: Closure and inverses are clear; $g^x=g^y\iff k\mid x-y$, so there are exactly $k$ distinct powers.

solutions.title: Subgroup of size k
solutions.body: *Subgroup:* $g^i*g^j=g^{i+j}\in\langle g\rangle$, and the inverse of $g^i$ is $g^{-i}=g^{kt-i}$ for any $t$ with $kt\ge i$, which is a power of $g$ (indeed $g^{kt}=e$). *Size:* $g^x=g^y$ iff $g^{x-y}=e$ iff $k\mid x-y$. So the powers $g^0,g^1,\dots,g^{k-1}$ are pairwise distinct and every other power equals one of them: $|\langle g\rangle|=k$. $\blacksquare$

answer: If $(g^i)^n=e$ then $k\mid in$, and $k\nmid i$, so $k\mid n$.

solutions.title: Prime order
solutions.body: Let $n=\operatorname{ord}(g^i)$. Then $g^{in}=(g^i)^n=e$, so $k\mid in$ by problem 2b. Since $k$ is prime and $1\le i<k$, $\gcd(i,k)=1$, hence $k\mid n$. Conversely $(g^i)^k=(g^k)^i=e$, so $n\mid k$. Thus $n=k$. $\blacksquare$

Let $g,b$ be elements of the same prime order $k$ in a group $(G,*)$. Prove that either $\langle g\rangle=\langle b\rangle$ or $\langle g\rangle\cap\langle b\rangle=\{e\}$. (You may use that $|\langle g\rangle|=k$ and that $g^i$ has order $k$ for $1\le i<k$.)
answer: If $g^i=b^j\ne e$ then $g=(g^i)^m=(b^j)^m\in\langle b\rangle$ for $im\equiv1\pmod k$, so $\langle g\rangle\subseteq\langle b\rangle$, and both have $k$ elements.

solutions.title: Either equal or trivial intersection
solutions.body: Suppose $\langle g\rangle\cap\langle b\rangle\ne\{e\}$: then $g^i=b^j\ne e$ for some $i,j$ not divisible by $k$. As $k$ is prime there is $m$ with $im\equiv1\pmod k$. Then $g=g^{im}=(g^i)^m=(b^j)^m=b^{jm}\in\langle b\rangle$, so $\langle g\rangle\subseteq\langle b\rangle$. Both sets have exactly $k$ elements, so $\langle g\rangle=\langle b\rangle$. $\blacksquare$

Suppose $|G|=56$ and $G$ is simple. How many Sylow $7$-subgroups does $G$ have, and how many elements of order $7$? (You may use problems 3a-3d: for a prime $p$, $\langle g\rangle$ has $p$ elements if $\operatorname{ord}(g)=p$, all non-identity elements of $\langle g\rangle$ have order $p$, and two such subgroups are equal or meet only in $\{e\}$.)

solutions.title: Sylow counting
solutions.body:
$56=7\cdot8$. By Sylow (i),(ii), $n_7\mid8$ and $n_7\equiv1\pmod7$, so $n_7\in\{1,8\}$. If $n_7=1$, the unique Sylow $7$-subgroup $P$ satisfies $f_h(P)=P$ for all $h$ by (iii), so $P$ is a normal subgroup of order $7$, contradicting simplicity. Hence $n_7=8$.

An element of order $7$ generates a subgroup of order $7$, which is a Sylow $7$-subgroup. Each Sylow $7$-subgroup has exactly $6$ elements of order $7$ (the non-identity elements), and different Sylow $7$-subgroups meet only in $e$ (problem 3d). So $G$ has $8\cdot6=48$ elements of order $7$.

**Answer: $8$ Sylow $7$-subgroups and $48$ elements of order $7$.**

Suppose $|G|=520$. Prove that $G$ is not simple. (You may use that, for a prime $p$, a Sylow $p$-subgroup of order $p$ contains $p-1$ elements of order $p$, and two different ones meet only in $\{e\}$.)
answer: If $G$ were simple, $n_{13}=40$ and $n_5=26$, giving $40\cdot12+26\cdot4=584>520$ elements.

solutions.title: Count elements of orders 13 and 5
solutions.body: $520=13\cdot5\cdot8$. Suppose $G$ is simple. For $p=13$: $n_{13}\mid40$ and $n_{13}\equiv1\pmod{13}$, so $n_{13}\in\{1,40\}$. If $n_{13}=1$ the unique Sylow $13$-subgroup is normal by (iii), contradicting simplicity; so $n_{13}=40$, giving $40\cdot12=480$ elements of order $13$. For $p=5$: $n_5\mid104$ and $n_5\equiv1\pmod5$, so $n_5\in\{1,26\}$, and as before $n_5=26$, giving $26\cdot4=104$ elements of order $5$. Elements of different orders are different, so $G$ would have at least $480+104=584>520$ elements: a contradiction. Hence $G$ is not simple. $\blacksquare$
